911: The sweet words of those who seek a man for his money, not from affection, end in sorrow.
912: Learn the character of the ill-natured who speak sweetly after learning your wealth — and keep away.
913: The false embraces of the wealth-loving are like hired mourners embracing a strange corpse in a dark room.
914: The wise who seek true grace never chase the hollow favors of the money-minded.
915: Those whose knowledge is polished by good sense do not covet trifling delights.
916: Those who would spread their own goodness do not desire the favors of those who bestow them on all who pay.
917: Only the unreformed covet the embraces of those whose hearts are elsewhere.
918: To the undiscerning, the embrace of the faithless is a trap as old as heaven's nymphs.
919: The jeweled arms of the mercenary are a hell that swallows the unguarded.
920: Treachery, liquor, and dice befall the one Fortune has left.
921: Those who always thirst for drink will inspire no fear in foes and lose the light of their fame.
922: Best not to drink at all. If you must, drink only if you care nothing for the good opinion of the great.
923: Drunkenness is shameful even before one's mother. What must it be before the wise?
924: The fair maid Modesty turns her back on those guilty of drunkenness.
925: Paying money to buy unconsciousness — that is what not knowing yourself leads to.
926: As the sleeping look like the dead, the drunk are but poison-eaters.
927: Those who drink in secret will have their secrets found out and laughed at by their townsmen.
928: Let the drunkard stop saying "I have never drunk." The moment he drinks, he betrays every past denial.
929: Reasoning with a drunkard is like diving under water with a torch to find a drowned person.
930: A sobering drunkard watching another drunk forgets his own yesterday.
931: Though able to win, do not desire gambling. Even the winnings are like a fish swallowing the hook.
932: Is there any livelihood that brings happiness to gamblers, who gain one and lose a hundred?
933: If a ruler is forever at the dice for gain, his wealth and its resources will pass into others' hands.
934: Nothing brings poverty like gambling — it brings miseries many and destroys one's good name.
935: Penniless are those so attached they never forsake gambling — the place, the dice, the game.
936: Those swallowed by the goddess called Gambling will never have hunger satisfied — and will taste hell hereafter.
937: Wasting time at the gambling-house destroys inherited wealth and goodness of character.
938: Gambling destroys property, teaches falsehood, ends benevolence, and brings misery here and hereafter.
939: Gambling prevents the attainment of five things: clothing, wealth, food, fame, and learning.
940: As the gambler loves his vice the more he loses by it, so the soul loves the body the more it suffers through it.
941: Too much or too little of food and work lets the three humors breed disease.
942: No medicine is needed for the one who eats only after the last meal is digested.
943: When the food is digested, eat with moderation. That is the way to lengthen life.
944: Assure yourself your food is digested, and never fail to eat when very hungry whatever is not disagreeable to you.
945: There is no disaster to one's life if one eats with moderation what does not disagree with one.
946: Pleasure dwells with the moderate eater. Disease dwells with the voracious glutton.
947: Numberless diseases afflict the one who eats immoderately, ignorant of the rules of health.
948: Let the physician inquire into the disease, its cause, and its cure — then treat faithfully by the rules.
949: The learned physician should note the patient's condition, the disease's nature, and the season — then proceed.
950: Medicine has four parts: patient, physician, medicine, and compounder — each with four subdivisions.
951: Thought, word, and deed agreeing, with the fear of wrong — these come naturally only to the nobly raised.
952: The high-born never swerve from three things: good manners, truthfulness, and modesty.
953: A cheerful face, liberality, pleasant words, and no reviling — these four are the marks of the truly high-born.
954: Though blessed with immense wealth, the noble will never do anything unbecoming.
955: Though their means fall off, the ancient families never lose their character for liberality.
956: Those who guard the honor of their families will not do what stains it.
957: A fault in a noble family shows like a spot on the evening moon.
958: If one of a good family betrays want of affection, their very descent is called in question.
959: As the sprout indicates the soil, the speech of the noble indicates their birth.
960: Whoever desires a good name must desire modesty; whoever would keep a family great must be humble to all.
961: Do no deed that degrades the family, though not doing it should cost your life.
962: Those who guard their honor will do nothing dishonorable even for the sake of fame.
963: In great prosperity, humility is fitting. In great adversity, dignity.
964: Those fallen from high position are like hair fallen from the head.
965: Even the hill-exalted are thought low if they do debasing deeds.
966: Why trail behind those who scorn you, waiting on their bidding?
967: Better to be said to have died in honor than to have lived on at the heels of those who scorned you.
968: For the high-born to keep the body alive when honor is gone is no remedy against death.
969: Those who give up life when honor is at stake are like the yak that dies at the loss of one hair.
970: The world will always praise the fame of the honorable who would rather die than suffer indignity.
971: One's light is the abundance of one's courage. One's darkness is the wish to live without it.
973: Raise the base as high as you will — they cannot become great. Bring the great low — they cannot become base.
974: The great remain the great while they are true to themselves.
975: However reduced, the great can still perform in the proper way deeds difficult for others.
976: It is never in the base's nature to seek the society of the great and take on their nature.
977: Even noble birth, wealth, and learning, in the base, produce only ever-increasing pride.
978: The great always humble themselves. The mean exalt themselves in self-admiration.
979: Freedom from conceit is the nature of true greatness. Obstinate self-praise is the nature of meanness.
980: The great hide the faults of others. The base only divulge them.
981: The truly good do good as if it were their nature — because it is.
982: The only delight of the perfect is goodness. All other delights are not delights.
983: Affection, fear of wrong, benevolence, favor, and truthfulness — the five pillars of perfect goodness.
984: Penance is the goodness that kills not. Perfection is the goodness that tells not others' faults.
985: Stooping to inferiors is the strength of the capable — the weapon with which the great turn aside foes.
986: The touchstone of perfection is to bear a defeat even from one's inferiors.
987: Of what avail is perfection that cannot do pleasing things even to those who pained it?
988: Poverty is no disgrace to one who abounds in good qualities.
989: Those called the shore of the sea of perfection never change, though ages change.
990: If there is a defect in the character of the perfect, even the great world cannot bear the burden.
991: If one is easy of access to all, it is easy to gain the virtue called goodness.
992: Warmth of affection and birth in a good family — these two make a proper behavior to all.
993: Resemblance of bodies is no resemblance of souls. True likeness is likeness of qualities that attract.
994: The world applauds the character of those whose usefulness comes of equity and charity.
995: Reproach pains even in play. The discerning show pleasing qualities even to those who hate them.
996: The world lives by touching the good. Without them it would sink into the earth.
997: He destitute of human qualities is a tree, though he may have the sharpness of a file.
998: It is wrong for the wise not to show good qualities even toward those who do only what is hateful.
999: For those who cannot rejoice, the wide world is buried darkness even at noon.
1000: The wealth of the goodless perishes like milk turned by water.
1001: He who does not enjoy the immense riches heaped in his house is to be reckoned dead — nothing is achieved by him.
1002: To know wealth can give every joy and still live blind and grasping — such a one is born a demon next.
1003: A burden to the earth are people bent on gaining riches and not true fame.
1004: What will the miser, liked by no one, regard as his own in the world to come?
1005: Those who neither give nor enjoy are truly destitute, though possessing immense riches.
1006: He who enjoys not his riches nor relieves the worthy is a disease to his wealth.
1007: The wealth of the one who never gives to the destitute is like a beauty growing old unwed.
1008: The wealth of the disliked is like a town tree's fruit — everyone takes, no one cares.
1009: He who only heaps up glittering wealth — others will take the hoards.
1010: The noble rich person's poverty is brief — a cloud that empties and refills.
1011: True modesty is the fear of wrong deeds. All other modesty is the bashfulness of virtuous maids.
1012: Food, clothing, and the like are common to all. Modesty is peculiar to the good.
1013: As the body is the abode of the spirit, modesty is the abode of perfection.
1014: Modesty is the noble's ornament. Without it, their pride would wound the world.
1015: The world regards as the seat of modesty the one who fears their own and others' guilt.
1016: The great make modesty their barrier of defense, not the wide world.
1017: The modest would rather lose life for modesty's sake than lose modesty for life's sake.
1018: Virtue will forsake the one who shamelessly does what others are ashamed of.
1019: Want of manners injures one's family. Want of modesty injures one's character.
1020: The actions of those without modesty at heart are like a puppet moved by a string.
1021: No greatness is higher than saying "I will not cease in my effort to raise my family."
1022: A family is raised by untiring perseverance in effort and wise contrivance.
1023: Even the Divine will take form and appear to help the one resolved to raise their family.
1024: Those prompt in efforts to better their family need no deliberation — such efforts succeed of themselves.
1025: People eagerly seek the friendship of the prosperous soul who has raised their family without foul means.
1026: A person's true manliness is making themselves the head and benefactor of their family.
1027: Among kin, the burden rests upon the strong.
1028: A family suffers from laziness and vain pride. For the striving, there is no wrong season.
1029: For the one guarding a family from harm, is it suffering alone the body must bear?
1030: If there are none to prop up a family in distress, it falls at the stroke of the axe of misfortune.
1031: Agriculture, though laborious, is the most excellent labor. However people wander seeking other work, they come at last to the farmer.
1032: Agriculturists are the linchpin of the world — they support all other workers who cannot till the soil.
1033: They alone live who live by agriculture. All others lead a cringing, dependent life.
1034: Farmers true to their soil wish their own king's flag over every land.
1035: Those who live by manual labor will never beg — they give to those who beg.
1036: Let the farmer's hands slacken, and even the sage's path fails.
1037: Let the land dry until a measure shrinks to a quarter — it will still yield plenty, even without manure.
1038: Manuring is better than ploughing. After weeding, watching is better than watering.
1039: If the owner does not personally attend to the cultivation, the land behaves like an angry wife and yields no pleasure.
1040: Maiden Earth laughs at the sight of those who plead poverty and live idle.
